title: Profit Is an Opinion, Cash Is a Fact
summary: The income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement answer three different questions: what was earned, what is owned and owed, and where the cash went. Depreciation, loan principal, capital spending, timing and deposits all separate profit from cash, and during construction the gap is at its widest.
body:
A profitable project can still run out of money, because profit is an accounting opinion about what you earned and cash is a fact about what is in the bank. Three statements, read together, tell you which one you are looking at.

Recall

Q. In Week 10, Vera taught you to read an appraisal's client, intended use, effective date and assumptions before its number. Why?

A. Because the number only means something in the context those four items set. An as-stabilised value prepared for a lender on stated assumptions is not the same thing as a market value today.

Q. Phase 1 ended with a checkpoint. What is your personal liquidity floor?

A. The cash you will not touch for any opportunity, however good it looks, so that a bad month never forces you to sell or borrow on someone else's terms.

Q. In Week 3 you learned that people respond to how they are paid. What is the principal-agent problem?

A. The gap between what you, the principal, want and what an agent you hire is rewarded for doing. A fee basis pulls the agent in a direction, so you design incentives and checks around it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Nadia here. Last week Sage taught you that a building is worth its net operating income divided by a cap rate. That is a statement about value. This week is about something more urgent: whether you can pay the bill due on Friday. Developers rarely fail because a project was unprofitable on paper. They fail because cash arrived later than bills did. A lender, an investor or a contractor can read your statements in five minutes and see what you missed. You need to read them faster than they do.

The three statements, in plain English

The income statement answers one question: over a period, say a year, did the business earn more than it spent? It lists revenue, subtracts expenses, and ends with net income, also called profit. It is built on the idea that income and expense belong to the period in which they were earned or incurred, whether or not money changed hands.

The balance sheet answers a different question: at one moment, what does the business own, what does it owe, and what is left for the owners? What it owns are assets. What it owes are liabilities. The difference is equity. Assets always equal liabilities plus equity, which is why it balances.

The cash flow statement answers the third question: where did the cash actually come from and go during the period? It sorts cash into three bins. Operating cash is cash from running the business. Investing cash is cash spent on or received from long-lived assets, such as land and construction. Financing cash is cash from lenders and investors, and cash paid back to them.

The professional framing is that the three are linked. Net income from the income statement flows into equity on the balance sheet. The cash flow statement starts from net income, strips out items that were not cash, adds in cash movements that were not income, and ends at exactly the change in the cash line on the balance sheet. If a set of statements does not tie together like this, something is wrong, and you should ask what.

Where profit and cash part company

There are five common gaps, and every one of them shows up in real estate.

  • Depreciation. The income statement spreads the cost of a building over its useful life as an expense. No cash leaves in that year, so profit is lower than cash.
  • Loan principal. Repaying principal is cash out, but it is not an expense, because it reduces a liability rather than consuming value. Cash is lower than profit.
  • Capital spending. Replacing a roof is cash out today, recorded as an asset, and expensed slowly through depreciation. Cash is lower than profit in the year you spend it.
  • Timing of collections and payments. Rent billed but not yet collected counts as revenue. A bill received but not yet paid counts as an expense. Profit and cash diverge by the change in what others owe you and what you owe them.
  • Deposits and money held for others. A condo buyer's deposit is cash in your trust account, not revenue, and often not yours to spend at all.

First worked example, hypothetical round numbers. A stabilised rental building earns net operating income of $600,000 a year. The owner pays $300,000 of loan interest and records $250,000 of depreciation. Ignoring income tax, net income is $600,000 minus $300,000 minus $250,000, which is $50,000. Now the cash. Start with the same $600,000, subtract $300,000 of interest, subtract $150,000 of loan principal, and subtract $50,000 spent replacing boilers. Cash left for the owner is $100,000. Profit says $50,000. The bank says $100,000. Neither is wrong; they measure different things.

Say that out loud now. Profit is an opinion. Cash is a fact. The cash flow statement is the bridge between them.

Why a development is the extreme case

During construction, the gap is at its widest. Second worked example, hypothetical. You spend $8,000,000 over three years building a rental project: land, hard costs, soft costs and interest. Under the usual accounting approach for a property being built for your own use or to hold, most of those costs are recorded as an asset on the balance sheet rather than as expenses. So the income statement for those three years may show almost nothing: no revenue and very little expense. A reader who looks only at profit sees a quiet company. The cash flow statement shows $8,000,000 leaving under investing activities and roughly the same amount arriving under financing activities, from your loan and your equity. The balance sheet shows an $8,000,000 asset that does not yet earn a dollar.

That is why a lender reads the cash flow statement and the balance sheet first on a development company, and why you must as well. The income statement tells you almost nothing until the building opens. Whether the accounting framework you use treats a cost this way is a question for your accountant; frameworks differ, and the treatment of interest in particular varies. Verify the treatment against the framework your statements are prepared under before you rely on it.

Time value: a dollar later is worth less

One more idea links the statements to value. A dollar today can be invested, so it is worth more than a dollar received in a year. That is the time value of money. When cash arrives late, its value today is smaller even though the total is unchanged. Nadia will work the arithmetic of net present value on Day 5. For now, hold the principle: the timing of cash, not just its amount, decides whether a project creates value.

How the best do it

Well-run property companies and contractors share one treasury habit a small developer can copy: a rolling short-term cash forecast, often thirteen weeks, rebuilt every week from actual bank balances, committed payments and expected receipts. It sits beside the monthly accounts, not instead of them. The accounts tell the board what was earned. The forecast tells the treasurer whether the company can pay its people and suppliers in week nine. You can run one on a single spreadsheet tab.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is managing your company by its profit and discovering, too late, that the cash is gone. It happens when collections slow, a draw is delayed, a deposit is locked in trust, or a principal payment lands in the same month as a big invoice. The control: a weekly cash forecast against every known payment and loan date, and your own minimum company cash balance, set in advance, that triggers action before the bank does.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads the income statement and stops. The second beginner's mistake is to treat net operating income as cash in the owner's pocket. NOI is before debt service, before principal and before capital replacements. The owner's cash is what remains after all three.

Callback

In Week 7, Warrick built your personal balance sheet and separated net worth from liquid net worth. The company works the same way. A balance sheet full of buildings is net worth. The cash line, and the forecast of what will be in it next month, is liquid net worth. A company can be rich in the first and broke in the second.

Recap

The income statement measures profit over a period. The balance sheet records what is owned, owed and left at a moment. The cash flow statement shows where the cash actually went, in three bins, and ties the other two together. Depreciation, principal, capital spending, timing and deposits all open a gap between profit and cash, and during construction that gap is at its widest.

Next: Ford, with Roman assisting, on Carillion, a contractor that reported profits until the month the cash ran out.
checklist: Read the cash flow statement and balance sheet before the income statement on any development company.
Check that net income, the change in equity and the change in cash tie together.
List the five gaps between profit and cash: depreciation, principal, capital spending, timing and deposits.
Never treat net operating income as cash available to the owner.
Ask which accounting framework the statements use and how it treats construction costs and interest.
Run a rolling thirteen-week cash forecast from actual bank balances.
Set a minimum company cash balance that triggers action before the lender does.
head: Field checklist
speak: A profitable project can still run out of cash, because profit is an opinion and cash is a fact. Three statements tell me which is which. The income statement measures what was earned over a period. The balance sheet shows what the company owns, owes and has left at a moment. The cash flow statement shows where cash actually went: operating, investing and financing. They tie together: profit flows into equity, and the cash flow statement ends at the change in cash. Five things separate profit from cash: depreciation, loan principal, capital spending, the timing of collections and payments, and deposits held for others. During construction the gap is widest, because costs sit on the balance sheet as an asset while the cash goes out. So I read the cash flow statement first, I forecast cash weekly against every payment date, and I keep a minimum cash balance that makes me act before the bank does.
terms: Income statement — the report of revenue, expenses and net income earned over a period, whether or not cash changed hands.
Balance sheet — a snapshot at one date of what a business owns (assets), owes (liabilities) and what is left for owners (equity).
Cash flow statement — the report of actual cash movements over a period, sorted into operating, investing and financing, that reconciles profit to the change in cash.

hostile.q: Your company shows a profit every year. Why is your cash balance falling?
hostile.a: Because most of our spending is on assets under construction, which the accounts record on the balance sheet rather than as expenses, and because we are repaying loan principal, which is cash out but not an expense. The cash flow statement shows it plainly: operating cash is positive, investing cash is heavily negative from construction, and financing cash covers the difference. I can show you the thirteen-week forecast against every draw and payment date, and the minimum balance at which I act.

title: Carillion: Profits on Paper, Cash Running Out
summary: Carillion, a large British contractor, reported profits until a July 2017 write-down and entered compulsory liquidation in January 2018. Its profits rested on estimates of how its long-term contracts would end while operating cash stayed weak and suppliers were stretched. The lesson is to put cash beside profit and believe the cash.
body:
Carillion reported profits right up until it collapsed in January 2018. The profits rested on estimates of how big contracts would end, while the cash kept going out. The lesson for an owner is simple: a reported profit that does not turn into cash on schedule is a question, not an answer.

Recall

Q. In Week 10, Sage worked backward from a finished building to the most you could pay for land. What is that figure called?

A. The residual land value: the value of the finished project, less every cost except land and less the developer's required profit.

Q. In Week 1, Ford took apart Berlin Brandenburg Airport. What was the core lesson about decisions?

A. That a project can be decided on a schedule and a budget that were never realistic, and that the later you admit it, the more it costs. Gates exist to force the admission early.

Q. Week 3's failure case was Champlain Towers South. What was its rule about?

A. When a qualified engineer reports a structural or life-safety defect, you fund and schedule the fix on the engineer's timeline, not the timeline that cost or comfort would prefer.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Ford here, with Roman assisting on the finance. You will hire contractors whose balance sheets you cannot see in full, and you will report to lenders and investors who rely on yours. Carillion is the clearest modern example of a company whose accounts said one thing and whose bank account said another. It was not a small firm. It built hospitals and maintained prisons and schools for the British state. If it could go from reported profit to liquidation in about six months, so can a contractor on your site. The facts below are drawn from public reporting, including a joint parliamentary committee report in May 2018. Where I am not certain of a detail, I describe it without a number.

Step 1: Timeline

Carillion was a listed British construction and support services group that grew through the 2000s, partly by buying other contractors. By the mid-2010s it held a large book of public and private contracts and paid its shareholders a dividend that rose for years. In July 2017 it issued a profit warning and announced a very large write-down on several construction contracts, and its chief executive stepped down. Further warnings followed that autumn. In January 2018, after lenders declined further support and the government declined to step in, the company entered compulsory liquidation. Tens of thousands of jobs, many subcontractors and several public projects were left exposed.

Step 2: Key decisions

Three decisions stand out. First, the group kept bidding for large, fixed-price construction contracts with thin margins and long durations, where one bad estimate can erase years of profit. Second, it stretched the time it took to pay suppliers, to as long as about four months by public accounts, while offering them an early-payment arrangement through banks. Third, it kept paying a rising dividend while its debt and its pension deficit grew. Each decision made the reported numbers look better in the short term and the cash position weaker.

Step 3: Assumptions

On a long construction contract, a contractor recognises revenue and profit as the work progresses, based on its estimate of the final outcome. That is legitimate, and it is how the industry reports. But it means the profit in any year is only as good as the estimate of how the whole contract will end. The key assumption was that troubled contracts would recover, through claims, variations or efficiency, to the margins forecast. Many did not. When the estimates were finally revised, profit already reported in earlier years effectively reversed in one blow.

Step 4: Incentives

Management pay, the share price and the dividend all rewarded reported profit and growth. A write-down hurts all three, so the natural pull was toward optimism in estimates and delay in recognising losses. Banks earned fees on the early-payment arrangement. Suppliers accepted long terms because they wanted the work. Nobody in the chain was paid to say early and loudly that the cash did not match the profit. That is Week 3's principal-agent problem at the scale of a whole company.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

The parliamentary report, and commentators before it, pointed to signals a careful reader of the statements could see. Cash generated from operations was weak relative to reported profit for years. Debt rose. A large part of the balance sheet was goodwill from acquisitions, an asset that cannot be sold to pay a bill. The supplier early-payment arrangement behaved like borrowing but was not presented as debt. And short sellers had taken large positions against the shares well before the first warning. Each is a gap between profit and cash, the gap Nadia taught on Day 1.

Say that out loud now. When profit and operating cash drift apart for years, believe the cash.

Step 6: Point of no return

Once the July 2017 write-down was announced, the company needed new money and the confidence of its lenders at exactly the moment its reported profits had just been shown to be unreliable. Every later step, asset sales, cost cuts and talks with banks and government, was a race against the cash running out. The point of no return was probably earlier than July: the moment the contracts became losses in reality but were still carried at their forecast margins. From then on, the longer the estimates held, the bigger the eventual hole.

Step 7: Root cause

Roman's reading, and mine: the root cause was running a cash-hungry business by its reported profit. The accounting method was not fraud in itself; estimating contract outcomes is normal. The failure was letting optimistic estimates stand while the cash told a different story, and funding the gap with stretched suppliers, borrowing and dividends the business had not earned in cash.

What it means on your site

Composite example, hypothetical round numbers. You hire a general contractor on a $20,000,000 project. Its last accounts show a profit, but its operating cash flow has been negative for two years, and it asks you to pay its monthly applications faster. Its subcontractors start calling your site superintendent about late payment. Those are the Carillion signals in miniature. Your controls: financial prequalification that looks at operating cash, not just profit; retainage and lien waivers; joint cheques or direct payment rights where your contract allows them; and a performance bond sized to the risk. Professional sign-off required: a construction lawyer for the payment and step-in provisions.

A second applied example. Your own company reports a profit on a condo project because revenue is recognised as units close, but closings are slipping and the construction loan matures in six months. On paper you are fine. In cash you are on a clock. The answer is the same: forecast the cash against the maturity and act on the forecast, not on the profit.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that the number everyone is rewarded for watching, profit, is the one that hides the problem. The control is to put operating cash flow beside profit on every report you read or write, and to ask in writing about any year where they diverge.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner prequalifies a contractor on revenue, profit and a reference list. The professional reads the cash flow statement, the age of its payables, and what its subcontractors say about being paid.

Callback

In Week 2 you learned the pre-mortem: imagine the project has failed and ask why. Run it on your contractor. "It is month fourteen and our builder has stopped paying its trades. What did we see in month two?" The answer is usually in its cash flow statement.

Recap

Carillion reported profit based on estimates of how its long-term contracts would end, while its operating cash stayed weak, its debt rose and its suppliers waited months to be paid. When the estimates were revised, the profits vanished and so did the confidence it needed to borrow. Rule 11: a reported profit that does not turn into cash on schedule is a question I ask in writing, not a figure I accept; I manage every project and judge every contractor by its cash.

Next: Priya on how the timing of cash moves your debt service coverage and your project's value.
checklist: Put operating cash flow beside profit on every financial statement you read.
Ask in writing about any year where profit and operating cash diverge.
Prequalify contractors on operating cash flow and payables age, not just profit.
Ask subcontractors directly whether they are being paid on time.
Treat goodwill as an asset that cannot pay a bill.
Look for financing that behaves like debt but is not shown as debt.
Protect your project with retainage, lien waivers, payment rights and a bond sized to the risk.
head: Field checklist
speak: Carillion was a large British contractor that reported profits until a July 2017 write-down and went into compulsory liquidation in January 2018. Its profits came from estimating how its construction contracts would end, which is normal, but the estimates were optimistic and the losses were recognised late. Meanwhile operating cash was weak for years, debt rose, suppliers waited months to be paid through an early-payment scheme that behaved like borrowing, and the dividend kept rising. When the estimates were revised, the profit vanished, and so did the lenders' confidence. The root cause was running a cash-hungry business by its reported profit. On my projects I prequalify contractors on cash, not profit, and I ask the trades whether they are being paid. My rule: a reported profit that does not turn into cash on schedule is a question I ask in writing, and I act on the cash.
terms: Percentage-of-completion accounting — recognising revenue and profit on a long contract as work progresses, based on an estimate of the final outcome.
Supplier early-payment arrangement — a scheme in which a bank pays a supplier early and the buyer repays the bank later; it can behave like borrowing.
Goodwill — the amount paid for an acquired business above the value of its identifiable assets; it cannot be sold separately to pay a debt.

hostile.q: Your contractor's accounts show a healthy profit. Why are you withholding a larger retainage than the market norm?
hostile.a: Because its operating cash flow has been negative for two years while profit was positive, and its payables are ageing. Profit on a construction contract rests on estimates of the final outcome; cash does not. Retention is commercial practice, not a standard, so I set it to the risk I can see. If the contractor shows me a year of positive operating cash and current subcontractor payments, I will review it.

rule: Rule 11: A reported profit that does not turn into cash on schedule is a question I ask in writing, not a figure I accept; I manage every project and judge every contractor by its cash.

title: When Cash Arrives Decides What It Is Worth
summary: The debt service coverage ratio tests the building's operating cash against interest and principal, so the same profit can pass or fail a loan. A year of delay reduces present value and the investors' annual return even when the price and profit are unchanged. The Wealth Ledger asks whether you could meet every project call on your worst month.
body:
Lenders and investors do not pay you for profit; they pay you for cash, and for cash that arrives on time. The same building can pass or fail its loan test, and be worth more or less today, purely because of when its cash moves.

Recall

Q. In Week 10, JAX defended an exit cap rate to a sceptical partner. What did he offer instead of a single number?

A. A range: a base, a downside and a severe case for the exit cap rate, with the deal shown to survive the downside.

Q. Phase 1's checkpoint returned to physiology. What is the red window on a night-shift schedule?

A. The hours, usually in the early morning, when alertness is at its lowest and errors are most likely; critical decisions should not be scheduled there.

Q. In Week 3, Sage taught you how anchors work. What is the defence against an anchor?

A. Calculate your own number first, such as the residual land value, so that the first number on the table is measured against yours rather than pulling you toward it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Priya here. Nadia showed you that profit and cash part company. My job is to show you what that gap costs, in the two currencies that decide whether you get financed and whether you create wealth: the lender's coverage ratio and the present value of your project. If you only look at profit, you will be surprised by both.

Debt service coverage is a cash test

The debt service coverage ratio, or DSCR, is net operating income divided by annual debt service. Debt service means every payment the loan requires in the year: interest and principal together. It does not care about depreciation, and it does not care about profit. It asks one question: does the building's operating cash cover the loan's cash demands, with room to spare?

First worked example, hypothetical round numbers. A building earns NOI of $600,000. The loan requires $300,000 of interest and $180,000 of principal a year, so debt service is $480,000. DSCR is $600,000 divided by $480,000, which is 1.25. Many lenders look for a minimum somewhere in that region on stabilised income property. That is commercial practice, not a standard, and it varies by lender, asset type and market.

Now change only the loan's amortisation, the schedule on which principal is repaid. Shorten it so the principal payment rises to $300,000. Interest is unchanged, so the profit the owner reports is unchanged too, because principal is not an expense. But debt service is now $600,000 and DSCR is exactly 1.00. The building covers its loan with nothing to spare, and most lenders would not make that loan. Same income, same profit, a different verdict, because the cash demand moved.

The professional framing: a lender sizes a loan from the cash test, not the profit test. When you read a term sheet, find the amortisation, the interest rate and the coverage covenant before you look at the loan amount, because those three decide how much cash the loan takes each year.

A dollar later is worth less

Nadia introduced the time value of money. Here is what it does to a developer. Suppose your finished project will sell for $10,000,000, and your investors require 10 percent a year on their money. Received in three years, that $10,000,000 is worth $10,000,000 divided by 1.1 three times, about $7,513,000 today. If a permit delay pushes the sale to year four, it is worth $10,000,000 divided by 1.1 four times, about $6,830,000 today. The sale price did not change. The project lost about $683,000 of present value because the cash arrived a year later.

That is before the extra year of interest, insurance, property tax and overhead you pay while you wait. Week 13's lesson on finance costs called that the line that grows while you wait. Put the two together and a one-year delay on a project like this can remove more than a million dollars of value without a single cost overrun on site.

Say that out loud now. The coverage ratio tests cash, not profit. A year of delay costs value even when the price holds.

Timing moves the return investors see

Investors also measure you by the internal rate of return, the annual rate at which the cash they put in grows into the cash they get back. Sage will teach it properly in Week 15. For now, see how timing alone moves it.

Second worked example, hypothetical. An investor puts in $1,000,000 and receives $1,300,000 back. If the money comes back after two years, the return is about 14 percent a year, because $1,000,000 growing at 14 percent for two years is about $1,300,000. If it comes back after three years, the return falls to about 9 percent a year. The profit, $300,000, is identical in both cases. The return the investor experiences is not. An investor who was promised the first and receives the second will remember it.

This is why the cash flow schedule in your pro forma is not a formality. When you show a lender or an investor a project, the months in which cash goes out and comes back are as important as the totals. A project with a smaller profit that returns cash sooner can be the better investment.

Where the timing goes wrong in practice

Four timing failures recur. Lease-up slower than planned, so stabilised NOI arrives later and the permanent loan cannot be sized in time. Condo closings delayed, so revenue is earned on paper but deposits and balances stay locked. Construction draws delayed by a lender's monitor waiting for documents, so you fund the contractor from equity. And retainage released late, which is a cash problem for your contractor that quickly becomes a schedule problem for you. Each one is a profit-neutral event with a cash cost. Model each one as a delay in months and look at what it does to DSCR, present value and the investors' return.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's short note for your personal balance sheet. Your share of a project's equity is net worth on paper. It is not cash, and you cannot pay a personal bill with it. When you are a guarantor or a co-investor, keep a personal cash calendar beside your company forecast: every date on which a project could call on you for money, such as an equity contribution, a cost overrun or a guarantee, set against the cash you actually hold. The question is not "what am I worth?" but "on the worst month in the next two years, could I meet every call without breaching my liquidity floor?" Any personal move, a guarantee, a new investment or a large purchase, needs that answer first. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal financial decision.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is underwriting a project on totals rather than timing: the costs and the revenue are right, but each arrives at a different time from the plan, and the loan fails its coverage test or the investors' return collapses. The control is a monthly cash flow in every pro forma, and a delay case in which lease-up, closings and draws each slip by a set number of months. If the project only works on time, it does not work.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner calculates DSCR with interest alone, forgetting principal, and believes the loan is safer than it is. The second mistake is to compare two projects by total profit without asking when the profit arrives.

Callback

In Week 10, Roman showed you that a refinancing gap opens when the value at maturity no longer supports the loan. Timing makes that worse. A building that stabilises a year late reaches its loan maturity with less income, a lower value and a weaker coverage ratio, all at once. The gap is not one risk; it is several risks arriving on the same date.

Recap

The debt service coverage ratio divides NOI by interest plus principal and tests cash, not profit; changing amortisation alone can move a loan from passing to failing. Delay reduces present value even when the price holds, and it reduces the investors' annual return even when total profit is unchanged. Model timing, not just totals.

Next: Vera on who sets the rules for financial statements, and what an audit really promises.
checklist: Calculate DSCR with interest and principal, never interest alone.
Read amortisation, rate and coverage covenant before the loan amount.
Build a monthly cash flow into every pro forma.
Run a delay case for lease-up, closings and draws.
Discount the exit value at the investors' required return to see what a delay costs.
Compare projects by timing of cash, not just total profit.
Keep a personal cash calendar of every possible call against your liquidity floor.
head: Field checklist
speak: Lenders and investors pay for cash that arrives on time. The debt service coverage ratio is net operating income divided by interest plus principal. A building with 600,000 dollars of NOI and 480,000 of debt service has a ratio of 1.25. Shorten the amortisation so principal rises, and the same building, with the same profit, can fall to 1.00 and fail the loan. Delay costs value too. A 10 million dollar sale received in year three is worth about 7.5 million today at 10 percent; received in year four, about 6.8 million. And an investor who gets 1.3 million back on a million earns about 14 percent a year over two years, but only about 9 percent over three. So every pro forma I build has a monthly cash flow and a delay case, and personally I keep a cash calendar of every call a project could make on me.
terms: Debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) — net operating income divided by annual debt service, meaning interest plus principal; a cash test of whether the building can carry its loan.
Amortisation — the schedule on which a loan's principal is repaid over time.
Time value of money — the principle that a dollar received earlier is worth more than a dollar received later, because it can be invested in the meantime.

hostile.q: Your pro forma shows a 2,000,000 dollar profit. Why should I care when it arrives?
hostile.a: Because you are lending against cash and your investors are measured on annual return. The same profit received a year later costs about a tenth of its present value at a 10 percent required return, and it adds a year of interest and carry. I show you the monthly cash flow and a case where lease-up and closings slip, so you can see the coverage ratio and the return in the delay case, not just the total.

title: Who Sets the Rules for Financial Statements
summary: Financial statements follow a named accounting framework, belong to management, and carry a level of assurance: audit, review or compilation. Different frameworks can produce very different profits from identical facts. Loan reporting covenants make the framework, assurance level and deadline binding.
body:
Financial statements are not just numbers; they are documents prepared under a named set of rules, by named people, with a stated level of checking. Before you trust a set of statements, or promise one to a lender, you need to know all three.

Recall

Q. In Week 10's review, Kema's Red Pen found a memo that deducted mortgage payments from NOI. Why is that wrong?

A. NOI describes the building's operations. Debt service depends on the owner's financing, so it belongs below NOI, not inside it.

Q. Phase 1's checkpoint revisited communication. What does bottom line first mean?

A. Say the conclusion and the decision you need in the first sentence, then give the reasons, so a busy listener can stop at any point and still have the answer.

Q. In Week 3, LEX explained misrepresentation. What turns a sales statement into one?

A. A false statement of fact, not vague sales talk, that induces the other side to enter the contract. Opinions and puffery are generally treated differently, though the details vary by jurisdiction.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Vera here. Records and evidence are my seat. A lender will lend you millions on the strength of a few pages of statements, and your loan agreement will require you to keep producing them on time, in a particular form. If you do not understand what kind of statements you are signing and promising, you can breach a loan without missing a single payment. You will also read other people's statements, a contractor's, a partner's, a seller's, and you need to know how much weight each deserves.

Who writes the rules: the accounting framework

In plain English, an accounting framework is the rulebook for how transactions are measured and presented. Two statements of the same company can show very different profits if they follow different rulebooks.

The professional framing: many countries use International Financial Reporting Standards, called IFRS, issued by an international standard-setting board. The United States uses its own generally accepted accounting principles, called US GAAP. Many countries also allow private companies to use a simpler framework designed for them; Canada, for example, has accounting standards for private enterprises. Some very small entities report on a cash basis or a tax basis, which are simpler still. Which framework a company may or must use depends on where it is, whether it is public, and what its lenders and investors require. Verify that against the primary source and your accountant before you rely on it.

First worked example, hypothetical. Two identical rental buildings each cost $10,000,000 and are now worth $12,000,000. One owner reports under a framework that allows investment property to be carried at fair value, with changes in value running through the income statement. Its profit this year includes a $2,000,000 gain that is not cash. The other reports under a framework or policy that carries the building at historical cost less depreciation. Its profit includes a depreciation charge and no gain. Same building, same cash, two very different profits. International standards do permit a fair value choice for investment property, while some other frameworks generally require cost; verify the current rule for the framework in front of you. The lesson for a reader: before comparing profits, ask which rulebook and which policy.

Who is responsible: management, not the accountant

Here is the rule beginners get backwards. The financial statements are management's statements. The owner or the board is responsible for them, for the records behind them and for the controls that make them reliable. An outside accountant may prepare, review or audit them, but responsibility for what they say stays with you. When you sign a representation letter to your accountant, or a compliance certificate to your lender, you are confirming that responsibility in writing.

Say that out loud now. The statements are mine. The accountant checks them; I own them.

How much checking: three levels of assurance

Assurance is the level of confidence an independent accountant adds. The names and exact standards differ by country, so treat these as concepts and verify the local terms.

  • An audit gives reasonable assurance. The auditor tests records, confirms balances with banks and others, examines evidence, and issues an opinion on whether the statements are fairly presented under the framework. It is the most expensive and the most reliable.
  • A review gives limited assurance. The accountant mainly asks questions and performs analysis, and reports whether anything came to their attention suggesting the statements are materially wrong. It is cheaper and lighter.
  • A compilation, sometimes called a notice to reader or a compilation engagement, gives no assurance at all. The accountant helps assemble the statements from the information management provides, without testing it.

None of the three guarantees there is no fraud. Even an audit is designed around material misstatement, not every error, and it relies partly on what management provides. Carillion, on Day 2, was audited.

What your lender's documents usually add

A loan agreement typically contains reporting covenants: promises to deliver financial statements by a deadline, at a stated level of assurance and under a stated framework, often with a compliance certificate showing the financial covenants, such as the coverage ratio, are met. Failing to deliver on time is commonly an event of default, even if every payment is current. Exact terms are negotiated; they are commercial practice, not law.

Second worked example, hypothetical. Your loan agreement requires annual statements reviewed by an independent accountant within 120 days of year end, plus a compliance certificate. To save fees, your bookkeeper arranges a compilation, and it arrives on day 140. You have breached two covenants: the wrong assurance level and late delivery. The lender may waive it, perhaps for a fee, or may use it as leverage at the next renewal. The fix costs far less in advance than afterwards: read the reporting covenant before you engage the accountant, and put the delivery date in your calendar with a margin.

Records behind the statements

Corporate law, tax law and your loan agreement each expect you to keep books and records: invoices, contracts, bank statements, minutes and the ledgers built from them. Retention periods and formats vary by jurisdiction and by purpose; verify the requirements that apply to you against the primary source. Practically, the statements are only as strong as the evidence behind each number. A cost you cannot document is a cost an auditor, a tax authority or a lender may refuse to accept.

Professional sign-off required: a licensed accountant, a chartered professional accountant or certified public accountant depending on where you are, for the framework, the engagement and any assurance report.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is promising a lender a kind of statement you cannot deliver, or relying on someone else's statements as if they carried more assurance than they do. The control: before signing a loan, list every reporting covenant with its framework, assurance level and deadline; and before relying on any third party's statements, find the accountant's report and read which of the three levels it is.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner sees an accountant's letterhead and assumes the statements were audited. Often they were compiled, which means nobody checked them. Read the report page first.

Callback

In Week 10 I taught you that an appraisal is only as meaningful as its client, intended use, date and assumptions. Financial statements are the same kind of document. Their framework, their date, the responsible party and the assurance level are the four facts that tell you what the number means. Read those before the number, every time.

Recap

Every set of statements follows a framework, belongs to management and carries a level of assurance: audit, review or compilation. Different frameworks can produce very different profits from the same facts. Lenders write reporting covenants that make the framework, assurance level and deadline binding, and missing them can be a default without a missed payment.

Next: Nadia, working net present value by hand, step by step.
checklist: Identify the accounting framework before comparing anyone's profits.
Remember the statements are management's responsibility, not the accountant's.
Read the accountant's report page to see whether it is an audit, review or compilation.
List every loan reporting covenant with framework, assurance level and deadline.
Engage the accountant at the assurance level the loan requires.
Calendar the delivery deadline with a safety margin.
Keep the documents behind every material number, and verify local retention rules.
head: Field checklist
speak: Financial statements are documents prepared under rules. First, the framework: international standards, United States standards, or a simpler private-company framework, and the choice can change profit a lot. Under one framework a building's rise in value can show up as profit; under another it is carried at cost and depreciated. Second, responsibility: the statements are management's, mine, not the accountant's. Third, assurance: an audit gives reasonable assurance, a review gives limited assurance, and a compilation gives none. My lender will turn all of this into covenants, requiring a certain framework, a certain level of assurance and a delivery date. Missing any of them can be a default even when every payment is current. So before I sign a loan I list every reporting covenant, and before I rely on anyone's statements I read the accountant's report page to see which level of checking it really carries.
terms: Accounting framework — the rulebook, such as IFRS or US GAAP, that governs how transactions are measured and presented in financial statements.
Assurance — the level of confidence an independent accountant adds to statements: reasonable for an audit, limited for a review, none for a compilation.
Reporting covenant — a promise in a loan agreement to deliver specified financial information, in a specified form, by a specified date.

hostile.q: These statements were prepared by a reputable firm. Why are you discounting them?
hostile.a: Because the firm's report says it is a compilation, which means the firm assembled the numbers from management's information without testing them. That is not a criticism of the firm; it is what the engagement was. I will rely on them for what they are, and I will ask for the bank statements, the rent roll and the major contracts behind the three numbers my decision depends on.

title: Net Present Value by Hand
summary: A step-by-step net present value calculation: lay out the timeline, choose a required return, compute discount factors, multiply and add. Two worked examples show that an option with less total cash can be worth more, and that a one-year delay at the same sale price can turn a profitable development negative.
body:
Net present value turns a stream of future cash into one number in today's dollars, at the return you require. If it is zero or positive, the project earns at least that return; if it is negative, it does not, however large the total profit looks.

Recall

Q. On Day 1 this week, what three bins does a cash flow statement sort cash into?

A. Operating, investing and financing.

Q. Phase 1's checkpoint revisited wealth mindset. What is the concentration ratio?

A. The share of your net worth tied up in a single asset or project. A high ratio means one bad outcome can take most of what you own.

Q. In Week 3 you learned sunk cost arithmetic. Why should money already spent not decide what you do next?

A. Because it is the same under every option you could choose from today, so it cannot change which option is best. Only future costs and future receipts can.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Nadia again. On Day 3 Priya told you that a year of delay costs value even when the price holds. Today you will calculate exactly how much, by hand, so that when someone shows you a spreadsheet you can check it on the back of an envelope. Net present value is the arithmetic behind every serious investment decision: whether to buy land, whether to build now or wait, whether to accept an offer today or hold for a higher price later.

The idea in plain English

If you can earn 10 percent a year elsewhere at similar risk, then $1,100 received in one year is worth $1,000 today, because $1,000 invested now would grow to $1,100. Working from the future back to today is called discounting, and the rate you use is the discount rate. Present value is a future amount converted to today's dollars. Net present value, or NPV, is the sum of the present values of every cash flow in a project, with money going out counted as negative and money coming in counted as positive.

The professional framing: the discount rate is your opportunity cost, the return you require for this level of risk. It is a choice, not a fact, and it should rise as risk rises. A positive NPV means the project beats that required return by the NPV amount, measured in today's dollars. The discount rate at which NPV is exactly zero is the project's internal rate of return, the subject of Week 15.

Step 1: Lay out the timeline

Write every cash flow against the year it occurs. Year 0 is today. Money out is negative. First worked example, hypothetical round numbers. You have two ways to invest $1,000,000 today.

  • Option A pays nothing in year 1 and $1,210,000 at the end of year 2. Total received: $1,210,000.
  • Option B pays $600,000 at the end of year 1 and $600,000 at the end of year 2. Total received: $1,200,000.

Option A returns $10,000 more in total. Most people stop there and pick A.

Step 2: Choose the discount rate

Suppose your required return for this risk is 10 percent a year. Write it as a decimal: 0.10.

Step 3: Calculate the discount factors

The discount factor for year t is 1 divided by 1.10 raised to the power t. For year 1, it is 1 divided by 1.10, which is 0.9091. For year 2, it is 1 divided by 1.21, which is 0.8264. For year 3, it would be 1 divided by 1.331, which is 0.7513. Each factor tells you what one future dollar is worth today.

Step 4: Multiply and add

Option A. The year 2 receipt is $1,210,000 multiplied by 0.8264, which is about $1,000,000. Subtract the $1,000,000 invested today. NPV is about zero. Option A earns exactly 10 percent a year and no more.

Option B. The year 1 receipt is $600,000 multiplied by 0.9091, about $545,455. The year 2 receipt is $600,000 multiplied by 0.8264, about $495,868. Together, about $1,041,322. Subtract the $1,000,000. NPV is about $41,322.

Say that out loud now. Option B returns less in total and is worth more today, because half of its cash arrives a year sooner.

Step 5: Interpret

At a 10 percent required return, Option B creates about $41,000 of value in today's dollars and Option A creates none. Option A's total is larger only because it holds your money longer, and you have priced your money's time at 10 percent a year.

Step 6: Test the rate

The answer depends on the discount rate, so test it. At 8 percent, the factors are 0.9259 for year 1 and 0.8573 for year 2. Option A becomes $1,210,000 times 0.8573, about $1,037,380, an NPV of about $37,380. Option B becomes $555,556 plus $514,403, about $1,069,959, an NPV of about $69,959. Both are now positive, because you are asking less of them, and B still wins. If the ranking ever flips as you change the rate, you have learned that the decision depends on your required return, and you must defend that rate explicitly.

Second worked example: a small development, on time and late

Hypothetical, unlevered, ignoring carry costs to keep the arithmetic clear. You buy land for $1,000,000 today. You spend $3,000,000 on construction at the end of year 1. You sell for $5,000,000 at the end of year 2. Total profit: $1,000,000. Your required return for development risk is 12 percent.

Discount factors at 12 percent: year 1, 1 divided by 1.12, which is 0.8929. Year 2, 1 divided by 1.2544, which is 0.7972. Year 3, 1 divided by 1.4049, which is 0.7118.

Present value of costs: $1,000,000 today plus $3,000,000 times 0.8929, which is $2,678,571. Total about $3,678,571.

Present value of the sale in year 2: $5,000,000 times 0.7972, about $3,985,969. NPV on time is about $3,985,969 minus $3,678,571, which is about $307,398. The project beats 12 percent, by about $307,000 in today's dollars.

Now delay the sale one year, to the end of year 3, at the same price. Present value of the sale: $5,000,000 times 0.7118, about $3,558,901. NPV is about $3,558,901 minus $3,678,571, which is about minus $119,670. The undiscounted profit is still $1,000,000. In present-value terms the project now destroys value against a 12 percent requirement, and that is before the extra year of interest, insurance and property tax a real delay would add.

Units and checks

Keep three habits. State the unit of every number: dollars, years, percent per year. Match the discount rate to the period; a monthly cash flow needs a monthly rate, not an annual one. And sense-check the sign: if a project with large early costs and late revenue shows a strongly positive NPV at a high discount rate, look for a sign error or a missing cost before you celebrate.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is choosing the discount rate to fit the answer you want. Lower the rate and almost anything looks good. The control: set your required return for each risk class in writing before you model the deal, and show the NPV at that rate and at two points above it.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner ranks projects by total profit, or adds up cash without discounting it. The second mistake is discounting year 0, the money spent today, which is already in today's dollars and takes a factor of one.

Callback

In Week 3 you learned that sunk costs cannot decide what you do next. NPV is the tool that enforces it. When you decide whether to keep going on a troubled project, discount only the cash flows from today forward. The money already spent appears in no option, so it appears nowhere in the calculation.

Recap

Lay out the cash flows by year, choose a required return, calculate the discount factors, multiply and add. A positive NPV beats the required return by that amount in today's dollars. Timing can reverse a decision: the option with less total cash can be worth more, and a one-year delay at the same price can turn a profitable project negative.

Next: Roman, in the room with a lender who asks why a profitable project is short of cash.
checklist: Write every cash flow against its year, with outflows negative.
Set the required return for each risk class in writing before modelling.
Calculate each discount factor as 1 divided by (1 plus the rate) to the power of the year.
Do not discount year 0.
Match the discount rate to the period of the cash flows.
Show NPV at the required rate and at two higher rates.
Check the sign and look for missing costs when NPV looks too good.
head: Field checklist
speak: Net present value converts future cash into today's dollars at the return I require, then adds it up, with money out as negative. At 10 percent, a dollar next year is worth about 91 cents today, and a dollar in two years about 83 cents. So 1,210,000 dollars in two years, on a million invested today, has an NPV of zero: it earns exactly 10 percent. Two payments of 600,000, in years one and two, total less but are worth about 41,000 dollars more today, because half the cash arrives sooner. On a small development, buying land for a million, building for three million and selling for five million in year two gives an NPV of about 307,000 dollars at 12 percent. Push the same sale to year three and the NPV turns negative, even though the profit is still a million. Timing decides value.
terms: Discount rate — the annual return you require for a given level of risk, used to convert future cash into today's dollars.
Present value — a future cash amount converted into today's dollars by dividing it by one plus the discount rate, raised to the number of periods.
Net present value (NPV) — the sum of the present values of all of a project's cash flows, outflows negative; positive means the project beats the required return.

hostile.q: Your NPV is positive, but only because you used an 8 percent discount rate. Why not 12?
hostile.a: You are right that the answer depends on the rate, so I show three. My required return for this risk class was set in writing before I modelled the deal, and here is the NPV at that rate and at two points above it. If the project only works at the lowest rate, I treat that as a reason to renegotiate the land price or walk away, not a reason to defend the lower rate.

title: Profit Up, Cash Down: The Annual Credit Review
summary: A scene in a lender's annual review: profit is up and cash is down. The lesson gives the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the question, when to stay silent and how to hold your state, with a one-page reconciliation that ties profit to cash.
body:
When a lender sees profit rising and cash falling, the question on the table is about arithmetic, but the question behind it is about trust: is money leaking out of the project it was lent against? Answer the arithmetic in one sentence, then answer the trust.

Recall

Q. On Day 2, what did Carillion's early-payment arrangement with suppliers behave like?

A. Borrowing. Banks paid suppliers early and the company repaid the banks later, which is debt in substance even if it is not presented as debt.

Q. Phase 1's checkpoint returned to hostile questions. What is the three-step pattern?

A. Acknowledge the question, bridge to what you know, then answer with the fact. Do not argue with the premise before you have answered.

Q. In Week 3 you met Cialdini's principles of influence. Which one is a lender most likely to use on you in a renewal meeting?

A. Authority and scarcity are common: the credit committee has the final word, and the window to agree terms is short. Recognising the principle lets you respond to the substance instead of the pressure.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Roman here, the lender's view. Every year a bank that lends to your company will review it. The credit officer will put your income statement beside your cash flow statement and look for the gap Nadia taught you on Day 1. If you cannot explain the gap calmly and with documents, the officer's report will say "liquidity concerns," and that phrase follows a borrower into every committee for years.

The scene

Hypothetical. Your development company has finished a 40-unit condo project. This year, 30 units closed, so the income statement shows a healthy profit. But the company's cash balance fell over the year. You are in the bank's office for the annual review of a $6,000,000 facility. The credit officer has your statements open and a pen in her hand.

She says: "Your profit is up and your cash is down by a lot. Walk me through it."

The question behind the question

She is not confused about accounting. She wants to know three things. Is the cash still in the business or has it gone to you personally? Is this project's money funding another project she has not approved? And will you be able to meet the facility's liquidity covenant, typically a minimum cash or net worth test, next quarter? Answer those three, in that order, and the meeting goes well.

The lines to say

Bottom line first, with a number and a place: "Three things explain it, and they add up to the full decrease. First, about $1,500,000 of buyers' balances from the last ten closings is still with the closing lawyers and arrives next month. Second, we repaid $2,000,000 of the construction loan, which is cash out but not an expense. Third, we put $1,000,000 of equity into the land for the next project, which your bank approved in March. Here is the reconciliation on one page."

Then hand over the page. It starts from net income, adds back non-cash items, shows the change in receivables, the principal repaid and the equity invested, and ends at the change in cash. It matches the statements to the dollar.

When she asks about the next project, say: "The equity came from retained profit after the loan was repaid in the order the agreement requires. No deposits and no loan proceeds from this project were used." Then stop.

Say that out loud now. Three items, one page, ties to the dollar.

The lines never to say

  • "That's just accounting." It tells her you think the gap does not matter, which is the one thing she is paid to test.
  • "Don't worry, it'll be back next month." A promise without a document is a hope.
  • "My accountant handles that." The statements are yours. Vera taught you that on Day 4.
  • Any figure you have not checked. If you are not sure, say "I will confirm that by Friday," and do.

When to stay silent

After you hand over the reconciliation, stop talking and let her read it. Silence while she reads is not awkward; it is respect for her process. If she frowns at a line, wait for her question rather than defending the line in advance. Borrowers talk themselves into trouble by answering questions that were never asked.

Second worked example: the harder question

She looks up. "Your receivable from closings is $1,500,000. What if three of those buyers fail to close?" This is a stress question, and the answer is a number. Hypothetical: three units at an average balance of $150,000 each is $450,000. Say: "If three fail to close, we keep their deposits under the purchase agreements, subject to the law and the deposit terms, and we remarket the units. The cash shortfall in the meantime is about $450,000. Our company cash after next month's receipts is $2,100,000 against a liquidity covenant of $1,000,000, so the covenant holds even in that case." You have answered with the downside, not with optimism, and you have shown the covenant headroom.

Whether you may keep a defaulting buyer's deposit depends on the contract, the deposit and trust rules and the local law; that is a legal question for your lawyer, and Week 41 covers it. In the room, say what the contract provides and that you have advice on it, not what you hope a court would decide.

Holding your state

A credit review feels like an examination, and the body reacts to examinations: faster breathing, a tighter voice, an urge to fill silence. Two practitioner habits help. Prepare the one-page reconciliation the night before, so the hardest part of the meeting is already done on paper. And before you walk in, while sitting still, take a few slow breaths with a longer out-breath than in-breath; many people find that settles the voice. These are habits, not medical advice; if stress affects your health, check that with your doctor. In the meeting, speak a little slower than feels natural and put the number first.

How the best do it

Experienced borrowers do not wait for the lender to ask. They send a short covering note with the annual statements that explains, in plain words, every material difference between profit and cash, with the reconciliation attached. The credit officer's report then quotes the borrower's explanation instead of writing its own. A small developer can do exactly the same with a one-page letter.

After the meeting

Within a day, send a short email that confirms what you said: the three items, the reconciliation attached, the receipts expected next month with their dates, and any figure you promised to confirm, with the date you will send it. A credit officer writes her report from her notes and from your documents. Make sure the documents say exactly what you said in the room, in the same numbers, so that the report she presents to her committee is the one you would have written. Then, when the closing balances arrive, send one line saying they have arrived and the cash position now matches the forecast. A borrower whose forecasts come true on the stated date is a borrower a committee trusts with the next facility.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is not the gap itself; it is an unexplained gap that a lender interprets as leakage. The control is to explain it first, in writing, with a reconciliation that ties to the statements, and to keep project funds visibly separate from company and personal funds.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner explains the gap with a story and no page. The second mistake is volunteering optimism, "sales are great," when the officer asked about cash.

Callback

In Week 6 you practised presenting numbers aloud and the line "I'll confirm by Friday." Use both here. Round the numbers, say the unit, put the decisive one first, and if a figure is not in front of you, commit to a date and meet it. A confirmed figure on Friday builds more credit than a guessed figure today.

Recap

The lender's question about profit and cash is really about leakage, cross-funding and covenant headroom. Answer with three items and a one-page reconciliation that ties to the dollar, answer stress questions with downside numbers, stay silent while she reads, and never call it "just accounting."

Next: Kema's week 11 review, with six questions, a Red Pen drill and a boardroom drill.
checklist: Prepare a one-page reconciliation from net income to the change in cash before any credit review.
Explain the gap in three items or fewer, each with a number.
Answer the trust questions: where the cash went, whether it funded another project, and covenant headroom.
Answer stress questions with downside numbers, not optimism.
Stay silent while the lender reads.
Never say the gap is just accounting.
Send a covering note explaining profit-to-cash differences with the annual statements.
head: Field checklist
speak: When a lender sees profit up and cash down, the real question is whether money leaked out of the project. So I answer the arithmetic in one sentence and then the trust. I say three items explain the full decrease: buyers' balances still with the closing lawyers, construction loan principal repaid, which is cash out but not an expense, and approved equity put into the next project. Then I hand over one page that starts at net income and ends at the change in cash, tying to the dollar. I stay silent while she reads. If she asks what happens when three buyers fail to close, I give the downside number and show the liquidity covenant still holds. I never say it's just accounting, I never blame the accountant, and if I don't have a figure, I commit to Friday and meet it.
terms: Liquidity covenant — a loan promise to keep cash, or another measure of liquidity, above a stated minimum.
Reconciliation — a schedule that shows step by step how one figure, such as net income, becomes another, such as the change in cash.
Leakage — money leaving a project or borrower for purposes the lender did not approve, such as other projects or personal use.

hostile.q: How do I know the equity in your next project didn't come from this project's deposits?
hostile.a: Because deposits never left the trust account, and I can show you the trust account statements and the closing lawyer's ledger. The equity came from retained profit after the construction loan was repaid in the order the agreement requires. The reconciliation traces each dollar, and I will give you the bank statements behind it.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 11 Review: Cash, Profit and the Red Pen
summary: Six questions on the three statements, the gaps between profit and cash, coverage, assurance and present value; a recap of the week; a Red Pen drill on a flawed year-end summary to a lender; and a two-minute boardroom explanation with a model answer.
body:
This week reduced to one sentence: profit is an opinion, cash is a fact, and the timing of cash decides what a project is worth. Today you test it, find the errors in a flawed cash summary, and explain it to a board in two minutes.

Recall

Q. On Day 3, what happened to the coverage ratio when only the amortisation changed?

A. Principal rose, debt service rose, and DSCR fell from 1.25 to 1.00, although NOI and reported profit did not change.

Q. Phase 1 closed with a checkpoint. What was the instruction for the phone recording?

A. Record a three-minute explanation and score it 1 to 5 for accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question.

Q. Week 3 closed with a review of the psychology of deals. What does loss aversion do to a seller?

A. It makes a loss feel larger than an equal gain, so sellers hold out for a price that avoids a paper loss even when selling is the better decision.

Why this matters

Kema here. Mr Shabazz, the three statements are the language every lender, auditor and investor will use with you for the rest of your career. A review is where five days of separate ideas become one tool you can use under pressure without notes.

The six questions

Question 1. Name the five common gaps between profit and cash. Answer: Depreciation, loan principal, capital spending, the timing of collections and payments, and deposits held for others.

Question 2. A building earns $600,000 of NOI, pays $300,000 of interest and $150,000 of principal, records $250,000 of depreciation and spends $50,000 on capital replacements. What are profit and cash to the owner, ignoring tax? Answer: Profit is $50,000. Cash is $100,000.

Question 3. What does Rule 11 say? Answer: A reported profit that does not turn into cash on schedule is a question I ask in writing, not a figure I accept; I manage every project and judge every contractor by its cash.

Question 4. What are the three levels of assurance, and which one checks nothing? Answer: Audit, which gives reasonable assurance; review, which gives limited assurance; and compilation, which gives none.

Question 5. At 12 percent, what is $5,000,000 received in two years worth today, and in three years? Answer: About $3,986,000 and about $3,559,000. A one-year delay costs about $427,000 of present value at the same price.

Question 6. A lender sees profit up and cash down. What is the question behind the question? Answer: Whether cash leaked to you or to another project, and whether you will meet the liquidity covenant next quarter.

Say that out loud now. Profit is an opinion. Cash is a fact. Timing decides value.

Speed round

Do these aloud, in your head, before checking. NOI of $500,000 with interest of $250,000 and principal of $150,000: debt service $400,000, DSCR 1.25. The same loan with principal of $250,000: DSCR 1.00. At 10 percent, the year 1 discount factor is about 0.91, year 2 about 0.83, year 3 about 0.75. So $1,000,000 in three years is worth about $751,000 today. An investor's $1,000,000 that becomes $1,300,000 earns about 14 percent a year over two years and about 9 percent over three. A building with $400,000 of depreciation and a $100,000 profit has, all else equal, more cash than profit. A $300,000 principal payment does the opposite: cash falls and profit does not move.

If any of those took you more than ten seconds, practise that one this week. Speed matters because, in the room, your attention belongs to the person across the table, not to the arithmetic. A number you can produce without effort is a number you can defend while listening.

Recap of the week

Nadia set out the three statements and the five gaps between profit and cash. Ford and Roman took Carillion apart: profits from optimistic contract estimates, weak operating cash for years, stretched suppliers and a rising dividend. Priya showed that coverage ratios test cash, and that delay costs value even when the price holds. Vera taught frameworks, responsibility and the three levels of assurance, and how loan covenants make them binding. Nadia worked net present value by hand. Roman put you in a credit review with a one-page reconciliation.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical year-end summary from a small developer to its lender. It has six planted defects. Find them before reading on.

Strong year. Net profit $900,000, so the company generated $900,000 of cash. Profit includes a $700,000 increase in the fair value of our rental building. Debt service coverage is 2.4, calculated as NOI of $1,200,000 over interest of $500,000. Condo deposits of $800,000 are included in cash available for the next project. The statements were prepared by our accountant and are therefore audited. Delivered on day 150; the loan requires day 120, but the bank never checks.

The defects. One: profit is treated as cash; they are different measures. Two: the $700,000 fair value gain is not cash at all, so the true cash from the year is far lower than the profit, and the summary does not say which framework allows the gain. Three: coverage uses interest only and omits principal, so the real ratio is lower. Four: condo deposits are counted as available cash, when they are commonly held in trust for buyers and not the developer's to spend; this is also a potential breach of trust and deposit rules. Five: "prepared by our accountant" is assumed to mean audited; it may be a compilation. Six: late delivery is admitted and dismissed; it is likely a covenant breach and an event of default whether or not the bank has noticed.

Boardroom drill

Explain this week in two minutes to a board that knows business but not development accounting. Then compare with this model answer.

"A development company can report a profit and still run out of money, so we manage by cash. Our income statement tells us what we earned, our balance sheet what we own and owe, and our cash flow statement where the cash actually went. During construction, our costs sit on the balance sheet as an asset, so the income statement looks quiet while millions go out. Lenders test us on cash: coverage divides net operating income by interest and principal together. Timing matters as much as amounts. A five-million-dollar sale that slips a year is worth about four hundred thousand dollars less today at our required return, before the extra interest. So every project has a monthly cash flow and a delay case, we forecast company cash thirteen weeks ahead every week, and we deliver statements at the assurance level and on the date our loans require. When profit and cash diverge, we explain it before anyone asks."

The biggest risk

The biggest risk after this week is reading statements in the wrong order: income statement first, and the cash flow statement never. The control is the habit: cash flow statement, then balance sheet, then income statement, then the accountant's report page.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner memorises the three statement names. The professional can trace one dollar of profit to the change in cash, and can say which gap explains every difference.

Callback

In Week 2 you started a decision journal. Add a line to it this week: for the next financial statement you read, write the profit, the operating cash, and the reason they differ, before you read anyone else's explanation. In six months the journal will show you whether your first reading was right.

Recap

Three statements, five gaps, one rule: believe the cash. Coverage tests cash. Present value prices time. Frameworks and assurance levels tell you how much a statement is worth. Explain the gap before anyone asks.

head: The six questions
speak: This week I learned that a profitable project can still run out of money. The income statement shows what I earned, the balance sheet what I own and owe, and the cash flow statement where the cash went, and the three tie together. Depreciation, principal, capital spending, timing and deposits all separate profit from cash, and during construction the gap is widest. Carillion showed what happens when a business is run by its reported profit while the cash stays weak. Lenders test cash: coverage is NOI over interest and principal. Timing decides value: a sale that slips a year is worth less today even at the same price. Statements follow a framework, belong to management and carry a level of assurance, and my loan covenants make those binding. My rule: a profit that does not turn into cash on schedule is a question I ask in writing.
terms: Operating cash flow — cash generated by running the business, before investing and financing movements.
Fair value gain — an increase in an asset's recorded value that some frameworks put through profit; it is not cash.
Event of default — a breach defined in a loan agreement that lets the lender exercise remedies, which can include a late report as well as a missed payment.

hostile.q: Your profit has risen three years running. Why does your operating cash flow lag it every year?
hostile.a: Because two of our largest profit items are not cash in the year they are recorded: a fair value gain on our rental building and closing balances still held by lawyers at year end. I can show you the reconciliation for each year. If the gap were growing without an explanation, I would treat it as you do, as a warning, and that is why we report it to you before you have to ask.
